extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biologists, and educated readers interested in evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the principles, conditions, and consequences of natural selection, divergence of character, and extinction, aimed at explaining how varieties become species over geological time. Uses analogies, examples (domesticated breeds, islands, fresh-water basins) and a generational diagram to illustrate processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Natural selection acts solely through the preservation of variations in some way advantageous, which consequently endure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as preservation of useful variations coupled with inheritance and the high geometrical powers of increase of species. Natural selection depends on favourable variations occurring and on competition (struggle for life) such that advantageous variants are preserved and multiplied. Sexual selection may aid ordinary selection by favouring the most vigorous/adapted males.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions favourable to natural selection (continental/island cycles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large continental areas that undergo many oscillations of level and exist for long periods in a broken condition are most favourable for producing many new forms likely to endure and spread widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin describes a lifecycle: continent → subsidence to islands (reducing intercrossing, allowing varieties to perfect) → renewed elevation to continent (severe competition enables spread of improved varieties). Key elements: large area, oscillation, periods of isolation, checked immigration, and time for varieties to be modified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation and confined areas slow competition and preserve forms
rubrics_metrics.description: On a small island the race for life will have been less severe, and there will have been less modification and less extermination. Confined areas expose inhabitants to less severe competition, allowing anomalous or ancient forms to endure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains persistence of 'living fossils' (e.g., Ornithorhynchus, Lepidosiren). Isolation reduces immigration and competition, permitting survival of forms that would otherwise be outcompeted on continents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fresh-water basins favour slow formation and survival of ancient forms
rubrics_metrics.description: All fresh-water basins, taken together, make a small area compared with that of the sea or land; consequently the competition between fresh-water productions will have been less severe, and new forms will have been more slowly formed, and old forms more slowly exterminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites seven genera of Ganoid fishes and anomalous forms in fresh water as examples; fresh-water habitats can act as refuges preserving relic lineages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection is slow, intermittent, and limited in scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection will always act with extreme slowness ... often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of the same region at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: favourable variations arise rarely and slowly; action depends on physical changes and checked immigration; free intercrossing retards the process. This slow, intermittent action accords with geological evidence of rates of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinction follows rarity produced by competition
rubrics_metrics.description: As each selected and favoured form increases in number, so will the less favoured forms decrease and become rare. Rarity, as geology tells us, is the precursor to extinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because environments are relatively fully stocked, increased success of one form inevitably reduces others. Fluctuations in seasons or enemies increase extinction risk for small populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common species more likely to produce favourable variations
rubrics_metrics.description: The species which are most numerous in individuals will have the best chance of producing within any given period favourable variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites evidence (chapter 2) that common species afford the greatest number of recorded varieties; rare species vary less and are beaten in the race for life by modified descendants of common species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of divergence of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Divergence of character: the more diversified the descendants from any one species become in structure, constitution, and habits, by so much will they be better enabled to seize on many and widely diversified places in the polity of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how slight differences between varieties can be augmented into large differences between species. Analogies: domestic breeding (pigeons, horses) where selection for extremes leads to divergent breeds. Natural selection preserves the most divergent (niche-expanding) variations because diversification allows access to more ecological places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection tends to preserve the most divergent variations
rubrics_metrics.description: In natural populations the importance of benefit being derived from divergence of character will generally lead to the most different or divergent variations ... being preserved and accumulated by natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin illustrates via a generational diagram: from a common, variable species a fan of diversified variations arises and the more divergent lines that reach ecological opportunities are preserved into distinct varieties/species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversification increases the number of individuals an area can support
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest amount of life can be supported by great diversification of structure; the more widely and perfectly the animals and plants are diversified for different habits of life, so will a greater number of individuals be capable of there supporting themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: sowing plots with several genera yields more biomass than with one species; farmers' crop rotation with different plant orders increases yield. Analogy to physiological division of labour in organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercrossing retards the action of natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The process will often be greatly retarded by free intercrossing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High rates of interbreeding between variants maintain intermediate forms and slow divergence; isolated or reduced intercrossing enables varieties to become well modified and perfected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection assists ordinary natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Amongst many animals, sexual selection will give its aid to ordinary selection, by assuring to the most vigorous and best adapted males the greatest number of offspring. Sexual selection will also give characters useful to the males alone, in their struggles with other males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual selection can produce characters not directly tied to survival but to mating success, accelerating divergence in some lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition strongest among closely related forms
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the most closely-allied forms ... which, from having nearly the same structure, constitution, and habits, generally come into the severest competition with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence, new varieties/species generally press hardest on their nearest kindred and tend to exterminate them; intermediate forms between earlier and later states often become extinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large genera/species groups vary and produce new forms more often
rubrics_metrics.description: In each country it is the species of the larger genera which oftenest present varieties or incipient species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: natural selection acts chiefly on forms that already have some advantage; the largeness of a group shows common inherited advantages. Thus large, successful groups are the main sources of new modified descendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite ecological 'places' limit indefinite increase of species
rubrics_metrics.description: As new forms are continually and slowly being produced, unless we believe that the number of specific forms goes on perpetually and almost indefinitely increasing, numbers inevitably must become extinct ... the number of places in the polity of nature is not indefinitely great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses this to explain why species number does not increase without bound; newly improved forms supplant others because ecological opportunities are finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified descendants tend to supplant ancestors (replacement-driven extinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most divergent and improved descendants of any one species will tend to supplant and exterminate in each stage of descent their predecessors and their original parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagrammatic explanation: later, more improved branches often take the place of earlier branches which fail to persist to higher generational horizons; only a few original species transmit descendants far into the future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological timescale consistency with slow divergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Each horizontal line in the diagram may represent many thousands to millions of generations (or successive strata); the slow, intermittent action of natural selection accords perfectly well with what geology tells us of the rate and manner at which the inhabitants of this world have changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin ties the generational diagram to the fossil record and strata, arguing that long periods and intermittent change explain observed affinities and intermediate extinct forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation preventing immigration is important for producing new forms
rubrics_metrics.description: When converted by subsidence into large separate islands ... immigration will be prevented, so that new places in the polity of each island will have to be filled up by modifications of the old inhabitants; and time will be allowed for the varieties in each to become well modified and perfected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation (geographic) reduces gene flow and competition from immigrants, creating ecological vacancies that favor local modification and speciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small and broken groups tend to disappear; large triumphant groups tend to expand
rubrics_metrics.description: Small and broken groups and sub-groups will finally tend to disappear. Looking to the future, we can predict that the groups of organic beings which are now large and triumphant ... will for a long period continue to increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictive consequence: ongoing success of large groups leads to continued expansion and extinction of many smaller lineages; but which groups ultimately prevail cannot be predicted with certainty.
